q: Calculate the frequency of allele b (q) on each island from the genotype counts.
Show that island X fits Hardy–Weinberg proportions.
p = 0.8, q = 0.2: p² = 0.64, 2pq = 0.32, q² = 0.04, which gives 64 : 32 : 4, exactly the counts.
Show whether island Y fits Hardy–Weinberg proportions.
Suggest two reasons why allele frequencies differ between the islands.
Any two: different selection pressures (background colour, predators); founder effect or genetic drift in small populations; different mutations.
Predict the effect of migration between the islands over many generations.
Gene flow would make the allele frequencies on the two islands more similar.
Identify the birth weight with the highest survival and name the type of selection shown.
3.5 kg; stabilising selection.
Explain how this selection affects the mean and spread of birth weight.
The mean stays the same but the variation is reduced, because both extremes are selected against.
Calculate the percentage of all babies that did not survive.
Suggest why very small and very large babies were less likely to survive.
Small: under-developed lungs, more heat loss. Large: difficult births, injury to baby and mother.
Suggest the effect of modern medicine on this selection.
Selection is much weaker, so over many generations the variation in birth weight may increase.

19.t: Working with data: snails and birds
q: Calculate q, the frequency of allele a, in generation 1.
Calculate p, and the expected number of heterozygous snails, in generation 1.
Calculate q in generation 5.
Thrushes eat more yellow snails. Explain the change in q.
Directional selection against the yellow phenotype: aa snails are removed, so fewer a alleles are passed on and q falls.
Explain why allele a is unlikely to disappear completely.
Most a alleles are hidden in heterozygotes, which are brown and protected; as q falls, very few aa snails appear for birds to remove.
